title: Divided by a common language
subtitle: gas station or petrol station, faucet or tap
summary: Recognise the everyday words that differ between American and British English - on the road, at university and around the home - and switch between them confidently.

lesson.heading: Two varieties, one language
lesson.text: Very few words and expressions are used exclusively in either British or American English, and you are likely to hear and read words from both varieties. Some differences are small: **street** has a wider range of meaning in American English, so an American may say *Let's cross the street here*, where a British speaker in a busy city would normally say *cross the **road***.

examples.text: *American:* Let's cross the **street** here; there's more traffic further down.

lesson.heading: Streets and roads
rows: in the US, a major road connecting different states
what you push round a supermarket
a bridge carrying one road over another

left.label: British English uses the
examples: Take **the M4** as far as Newbury, then turn off on to **the A34** for Oxford.

right.label: American English uses no article
examples: Take **I-45** north for about 20 miles, then take **25** west.

lesson.heading: Educational terminology
rows: My older brother never went to **college**.
My older brother never went to **university**. (a British college is usually a place of specialised education for people over 16)
What **modules** are you taking next **semester** or **term**?
Most of my friends are **third years**.
My **professors** are all very friendly. (a general term for university teachers)
My **lecturers** are all very friendly. (a professor holds the highest academic rank)
I want to be an **elementary school** teacher.
I want to be a **primary school** teacher.
My years in **high school** were not very happy.
My years in **secondary school** were not very happy.
lesson.note: A sophomore is in the second year of study; a junior in the third.

lesson.heading: Around the home
rows: the cable that takes electricity safely into the ground
a large metal container for rubbish
the kitchen equipment you cook food on

lesson.heading: Same word, different world
lesson.text: Some words exist in both varieties but point to different things. If an American says they are going to **college** next year, they usually mean university; a British speaker probably means an institution for students over 16 learning a particular skill, such as a teacher-training college. **Professor** is an appropriate way to address any university teacher in the US, but in Britain it is a title given only to those of the highest academic rank.

examples.text: A **primary school** teacher in Britain teaches more or less the same age group as an **elementary school** teacher in the US.
You register for a **module** in Britain and for a **course** in the US.
If someone says they are **majoring in** psychology, they mean psychology is their main subject of study.

lesson.text: Choose one variety and stay in it inside a single piece of writing - mixing gas station with flyover sounds odd to both audiences.

exercises.prompt: 'I lost my way at the big intersection just south of the city.' Who is speaking?
options: an American - a British speaker would say junction
a British speaker - an American would say junction
an American - a British speaker would say overpass
a British speaker - an American would say crosswalk
exercises.explanation: Intersection is American; the British word is junction.

exercises.prompt: 'Why are there always so many shopping trolleys left in the car park?' Who is speaking?
options: a British speaker - an American would say shopping carts in the parking lot
an American - a British speaker would say shopping carts in the parking lot
a British speaker - an American would say trolleys in the lot
an American - a British speaker would say trolleys in the car park
exercises.explanation: Trolley and car park are British; cart and parking lot are American.

exercises.prompt: 'Cross the road at the pedestrian crossing, then turn left.' How would an American say it?
options: Cross the street at the crosswalk, then take a left.
Cross the road at the crosswalk, then turn left.
Cross the street at the pedestrian crossing, then take a left.
Cross the trail at the crosswalk, then back up.
exercises.explanation: Street, crosswalk and take a left are all American.

exercises.prompt: American: You can't drive any further; you'll have to back up, the street is very narrow. British: You can't drive any further; you'll have to ___, the road is very narrow.
exercises.explanation: Americans back up; British speakers reverse.

exercises.prompt: British: You'll see the petrol station just after the flyover. American: You'll see the ___ station just after the overpass.
exercises.explanation: American English has gas station and overpass for petrol station and flyover.

exercises.prompt: American: Once you get on to the Interstate, it will only take two hours. British: Once you get on to the ___, it will only take two hours.
exercises.explanation: An Interstate is the US equivalent of a British motorway.

exercises.prompt: American: The office is kitty-corner to the Chinese restaurant. British: The office is ___ opposite the Chinese restaurant.
exercises.explanation: Kitty-corner is informal American English for diagonally opposite.

exercises.prompt: American: There's a creek at the end of the trail. British: There's a stream at the end of the ___.
exercises.explanation: A trail is a path and a creek is a stream or small river.

exercises.prompt: Match each American word with its British equivalent.
Match each American education word with its British equivalent.
Is each word American English or British English?
What year of study are you in if you are a sophomore?
options: the second year
the first year
the third year
the final year
exercises.explanation: Freshman, sophomore and junior are the first, second and third years.

exercises.prompt: If someone says they are majoring in psychology, what do they mean?
options: psychology is their main subject of study
they teach psychology
they are in their final year
they take psychology as an extra option
exercises.explanation: Major in is the American equivalent of doing honours in a subject.

exercises.statement: A primary school teacher teaches at more or less the same level as an elementary school teacher.
exercises.explanation: Correct - elementary school is the American equivalent of British primary school.

exercises.statement: If an American says they're going to college next year, it means the same as when a British person says it.
exercises.explanation: In the US it usually means going to university; in Britain it is likely to mean an institution for students over 16 learning a special skill.

exercises.statement: Someone who says they are a secondary school teacher is more likely to be British than American.

exercises.prompt: Calling a university teacher 'Professor' in Britain is different from in the US because ___.
options: in Britain it is a title only for those of the highest academic rank
in Britain it is used only for primary teachers
in the US it is considered rude
in Britain it means a research student
exercises.explanation: In the US Professor is an appropriate form of address for any university teacher.

exercises.prompt: Put this British set of directions in order.
exercises.answer: Take the M4 as far as Newbury, then turn off on to the A34
exercises.explanation: British road numbers take the; American ones do not.
